statement: In declarative sentences with nominal subject and object, the dominant order is almost always one in which the subject precedes the object.
antecedent: declarative sentence with nominal subject and object
consequent: subject precedes object in dominant order

statement: In languages with prepositions, the genitive almost always follows the governing noun, while in languages with postpositions it almost always precedes.
antecedent: language has prepositions
consequent: genitive follows the governing noun

statement: In languages with postpositions, the genitive almost always precedes the governing noun.
antecedent: language has postpositions
consequent: genitive precedes the governing noun

statement: Languages with dominant VSO order are always prepositional.
antecedent: language has dominant VSO word order
consequent: language uses prepositions

statement: With overwhelmingly greater than chance frequency, languages with normal SOV order are postpositional.
antecedent: language has dominant SOV word order
consequent: language uses postpositions

statement: If a language has dominant SOV order and the genitive follows the governing noun, then the adjective likewise follows the noun.
antecedent: language has dominant SOV order AND the genitive follows the governing noun
consequent: adjective follows the noun

statement: All languages with dominant VSO order have SVO as an alternative or as the only alternative basic order.
antecedent: language has dominant VSO order
consequent: language has SVO as alternative or only alternative basic order

statement: If in a language with dominant SOV order there is no alternative basic order, then all adverbial modifiers of the verb likewise precede the verb.
antecedent: language has dominant SOV order with no alternative basic order
consequent: all adverbial modifiers of the verb precede the verb

statement: When a yes-no question is marked by a single morpheme, it is always differentiated from the corresponding declarative by intonation or by a characteristic position of the morpheme at the beginning or end of the sentence.
antecedent: yes-no question is marked by a single morpheme
consequent: the question morpheme is differentiated from declarative by intonation or by sentence-peripheral position

statement: With well more than chance frequency, when question particles or affixes are specified in position by reference to the sentence as a whole, if initial they are found in prepositional languages and if final in postpositional.
antecedent: question particles or affixes are sentence-initial
consequent: language is prepositional

statement: Question particles or affixes, when specified in position by reference to a particular word in the sentence, almost always follow that word. Such particles do not occur in languages with dominant order VSO.
antecedent: question particle or affix is positioned relative to a particular word
consequent: the particle follows that word

statement: Inversion of statement order so that verb precedes subject occurs only in languages where the question word or phrase is normally initial. This same inversion occurs in yes-no questions only if it also occurs in interrogative word questions.
antecedent: verb-subject inversion occurs in yes-no questions
consequent: verb-subject inversion also occurs in interrogative word questions

statement: If a language has dominant order VSO in declarative sentences, it always puts interrogative words or phrases first in interrogative word questions; if it has dominant order SOV, there is never such an invariant rule.
antecedent: language has dominant VSO order in declarative sentences
consequent: interrogative words or phrases are always placed first in interrogative word questions

statement: If the nominal object always precedes the verb, then verb forms subordinate to the main verb also precede it.
antecedent: nominal object always precedes the verb (i.e. dominant OV order)
consequent: subordinate verb forms also precede the main verb

statement: In conditional statements, the conditional clause precedes the conclusion as the normal order in all languages.
antecedent: language has conditional statements
consequent: conditional clause precedes the conclusion as normal order

statement: In expressions of volition and purpose, a subordinate verbal form always follows the main verb as the normal order except in those languages in which the nominal object always precedes the verb.
antecedent: language expresses volition or purpose with a subordinate verbal form AND the nominal object does not always precede the verb
consequent: the subordinate verbal form follows the main verb as normal order

statement: In languages with dominant order SOV, an inflected auxiliary always follows the main verb. In languages with dominant order VSO, an inflected auxiliary always precedes the main verb.
antecedent: language has dominant SOV order
consequent: inflected auxiliary follows the main verb

statement: In languages with dominant order VSO, an inflected auxiliary always precedes the main verb.
antecedent: language has dominant VSO order
consequent: inflected auxiliary precedes the main verb

statement: With overwhelmingly more than chance frequency, languages with dominant order VSO have the adjective after the noun.
antecedent: language has dominant VSO order
consequent: adjective follows the noun

statement: When the descriptive adjective precedes the noun, the demonstrative and the numeral, with overwhelmingly more than chance frequency, do likewise.
antecedent: descriptive adjective precedes the noun
consequent: demonstrative and numeral also precede the noun

statement: When the general rule is that the descriptive adjective follows, there may be a minority of adjectives which usually precede, but when the general rule is that descriptive adjectives precede, there are no exceptions.
antecedent: the dominant rule is that descriptive adjectives precede the noun
consequent: there are no exceptions (no adjectives that follow)

statement: When any or all of the items—demonstrative, numeral, and descriptive adjective—precede the noun, they are always found in that order. If they follow, the order is either the same or its exact opposite.
antecedent: demonstrative, numeral, and descriptive adjective all precede the noun
consequent: their relative order is always demonstrative > numeral > adjective > noun

statement: If some or all adverbs follow the adjective they modify, then the adjective follows the noun and the verb precedes its nominal object as the dominant order.
antecedent: some or all adverbs follow the adjective they modify
consequent: adjective follows the noun AND verb precedes its nominal object as dominant order

statement: If in comparisons of superiority the only order, or one of the alternative orders, is standard-marker-adjective, then the language is postpositional. With overwhelmingly more than chance frequency, if the only order is adjective-marker-standard, the language is prepositional.
antecedent: the only or one of the alternative orders in comparisons of superiority is standard-marker-adjective
consequent: language is postpositional

statement: If in apposition the proper noun usually precedes the common noun, then the language is one in which the governing noun precedes its dependent genitive. With much better than chance frequency, if the common noun usually precedes the proper noun, the dependent genitive precedes its governing noun.
antecedent: in apposition the proper noun usually precedes the common noun
consequent: governing noun precedes its dependent genitive

statement: If the relative expression precedes the noun, either the language is postpositional, or the adjective precedes the noun, or both.
antecedent: relative expression (relative clause) precedes the noun
consequent: language is postpositional OR adjective precedes the noun (or both)

statement: If the pronominal object follows the verb, so does the nominal object.
antecedent: pronominal object follows the verb
consequent: nominal object also follows the verb

statement: If a language has discontinuous affixes, it always has either prefixing or suffixing or both.
antecedent: language has discontinuous affixes (circumfixes or similar)
consequent: language also has prefixing or suffixing or both

statement: If a language is exclusively suffixing, it is postpositional; if it is exclusively prefixing, it is prepositional.
antecedent: language is exclusively suffixing
consequent: language is postpositional

statement: If a language is exclusively prefixing, it is prepositional.
antecedent: language is exclusively prefixing
consequent: language is prepositional

statement: If both the derivation and inflection follow the root, or they both precede the root, the derivation is always between the root and the inflection.
antecedent: both derivation and inflection follow the root, OR both precede the root
consequent: derivation is always positioned between the root and the inflection

statement: If a language has inflection, it always has derivation.
antecedent: language has inflectional morphology
consequent: language also has derivational morphology

statement: If the verb has categories of person-number or of gender, it always has tense-mode categories.
antecedent: verb has categories of person-number or of gender
consequent: verb also has tense-mode (tense or mood) categories

statement: If either the subject or object noun agrees with the verb in gender, then the adjective always agrees with the noun in gender.
antecedent: subject noun or object noun agrees with the verb in gender
consequent: adjective agrees with the noun in gender

statement: Whenever the verb agrees with a nominal subject or nominal object in gender, it also agrees with them in number.
antecedent: verb agrees with nominal subject or object in gender
consequent: verb also agrees with them in number

statement: When number agreement between the noun and verb is suspended and the rule is based on order, the case is always one in which the verb precedes and is in the singular.
antecedent: number agreement between noun and verb is suspended and the rule is based on word order
consequent: the case is one where the verb precedes the noun and is in the singular

statement: No language has a trial number unless it has a dual. No language has a dual unless it has some nonsingular number categories.
antecedent: language has a trial number category
consequent: language also has a dual number category

statement: No language has a dual unless it has some nonsingular number category.
antecedent: language has a dual number category
consequent: language has at least one other nonsingular number category

statement: There is no language in which the plural does not have some nonzero allomorphs, whereas there are languages in which the singular is expressed only by zero.
antecedent: language has a plural category
consequent: plural has at least some nonzero allomorphs

statement: If a language has the category of gender, it always has the category of number.
antecedent: language has grammatical gender
consequent: language also has grammatical number

statement: A language never has more gender categories in nonsingular numbers than in the singular.
antecedent: language has gender categories
consequent: number of gender distinctions in nonsingular is less than or equal to number of gender distinctions in singular

statement: Where there is a case system, the only case which ever has only zero allomorphs is the one which includes among its meanings that of the subject of the intransitive verb (the unmarked nominative or absolutive).
antecedent: language has a case system with a case that has only zero allomorphs
consequent: that zero-allomorph case is the one that includes the meaning of subject of intransitive verb

statement: Where morphemes of both number and case are present and both follow or both precede the noun base, the expression of number almost always comes between the noun base and the expression of case.
antecedent: language has both number and case morphemes and both occupy the same side of the noun base
consequent: the number morpheme is positioned between the noun base and the case morpheme

statement: When the adjective follows the noun, the adjective expresses all the inflectional categories of the noun. In such cases the verb may lack overt expression of one or all of these categories.
antecedent: adjective follows the noun
consequent: adjective expresses all inflectional categories of the noun

statement: If in a language the verb follows both the nominal subject and nominal object as the dominant order, the language almost always has a case system.
antecedent: language has dominant SOV order (verb follows both subject and object)
consequent: language has a morphological case system

statement: All languages have pronominal categories involving at least three persons and two numbers.
antecedent: any language
consequent: language has at least three person distinctions and two number distinctions in pronouns

statement: If a language has gender categories in the noun, it has gender categories in the pronoun.
antecedent: language has grammatical gender distinctions in nouns
consequent: language also has grammatical gender distinctions in pronouns

statement: If a language has gender distinctions in the first person, it always has gender distinctions in the second or third person, or in both.
antecedent: language has gender distinctions in first person pronouns
consequent: language has gender distinctions in second person pronouns or third person pronouns or both

statement: If there are any gender distinctions in the plural of the pronoun, there are some gender distinctions in the singular also.
antecedent: language has gender distinctions in plural pronouns
consequent: language has gender distinctions in singular pronouns
